html:
Among the equipment needed for astrophotography, there is obviously the instrument that turns light into an analog signal.

Two main choices are available to us:

1- a CCD camera.
2- a digital SLR camera.

CCD cameras are more complex to operate and cost more. On the other hand, they are more sensitive and produce less noise, which is a very big advantage.

For practical and price reasons, I chose a digital SLR camera. The model I went with is a Canon 40D with a 10.1 megapixel APS-C sensor. Canon cameras are preferred by amateur astronomers for certain qualities such as:

- The ability to record images in true raw format, meaning that what is recorded is what the sensor received.
- Relatively lower thermal noise at a given gain (ISO).

The 40D also has other qualities that make it a camera of choice for astrophotography, in particular the ability to control the camera remotely and "Live View", which lets you focus quickly by seeing the image the sensor is receiving.

Normally, the sensors of digital cameras are fitted with a filter that cuts infrared and ultraviolet. Since many objects in the sky emit in the red, this filter removes part of the emitted light, which is not desirable. So the filter in front of the sensor is removed and replaced either with a UV/IR filter that lets red through, with a clear glass that allows autofocus, or with nothing at all.

I chose the third option, that is nothing at all. The drawback of this option is that autofocus no longer focuses in the right place. That's not a big problem, since in astrophotography autofocus is never used. The advantage of the option is that there is less glass in the light path and therefore a better signal. Also, the camera can be used for infrared photography, which is pretty interesting.

It was Jaques Chagnon who modified my 40D.

Here are a few pictures of the 40D. Note the Hutech IDAS-LPS "clip-on" filter in position (blue in the picture). This filter cuts the light emitted by artificial light sources such as mercury or sodium lamps. It lets me shoot from home without feeling (in the photos) the effects of light pollution.
